1.q: וְ⁠אִשָּׁ֣ה אַחַ֣ת מִ⁠נְּשֵׁ֣י בְנֵֽי־הַ֠⁠נְּבִיאִים צָעֲקָ֨ה אֶל־אֱלִישָׁ֜ע
1.note: The author is introducing this **woman** as a new participant in the story. If your language has its own way of introducing new participants, you could use it here in your translation. Alternate translation: [Now a certain woman, the widow of one of the sons of the prophets, cried out to Elisha]
See how you decided at 3:7 to represent the term **saying** when it introduces a direct quotation.

The woman is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you know** already includes this meaning. She is doing that to emphasize Elisha’s personal awareness of her late husband’s faith. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and you know personally]

2.q: אֵ֣ין לְ⁠שִׁפְחָתְ⁠ךָ֥ כֹל֙ בַּ⁠בַּ֔יִת כִּ֖י אִם־אָס֥וּךְ שָֽׁמֶן
2.note: If it would appear in your language that the woman was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [The only thing your maidservant has in the house is a jar of oil]

The woman is speaking of herself in the third person as **your maidservant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [me, your maidservant,]

3.note: Elisha is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a term, **few**, that is the opposite of his intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [Get as many as you can]

4.note: Since the woman uses the term “children” in [4:1](ta:04), it is likely that the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense here that includes both boys and girls. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that indicates that, here and verses 5 and 7. Alternate translation: [your children]

Elisha is using the adjective **full** as a noun to mean a certain kind of vessel or container. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [And the full vessel, set aside] or [And once a vessel is full, set it aside]

Elisha assumes that the widow will understand that she should continue pouring oil into each container until it is full before moving on to the next one and that she should set each full container aside to make room for filling empty ones. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And once a vessel is full, set it aside and fill another vessel]

5.note: The author assumes that readers will understand that the woman followed Elisha’s instructions in verse 3 to borrow containers from her neighbors before she returned home and shut the door. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And she went from him and asked for empty vessels from all of her neighbors, then came home and shut the door]

7.note: The word **you** is singular in both of these instances because Elisha is addressing the woman directly. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

8.note: The author is using the phrase translated **And it was the day** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
The author is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [some food … some food]

9.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:9.

10.note: This expression most likely refers to a room that the woman and her husband built on the flat roof of their house with walls on all sides for privacy and protection from the weather. The roof would have been reached by an exterior stairway, so Elisha would have had privacy, and his comings and goings would not have disturbed the household. You may be able to describe this room in terms of your own culture.

11.note: The author is using the phrase translated **And it was the day** to introduce a new development within this account of the Shunammite woman. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new development.

12.note: See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Kings of how the author and characters may use the term “face” to mean “in front of.” Alternate translation: [in front of him] or [near his room]

13.q: אֱמָר־נָ֣א אֵלֶי⁠הָ֮ הִנֵּ֣ה חָרַ֣דְתְּ ׀ אֵלֵי⁠נוּ֮ אֶת־כָּל־הַ⁠חֲרָדָ֣ה הַ⁠זֹּאת֒ מֶ֚ה לַ⁠עֲשׂ֣וֹת לָ֔⁠ךְ הֲ⁠יֵ֤שׁ לְ⁠דַבֶּר־לָ⁠ךְ֙ אֶל־הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ א֖וֹ אֶל־שַׂ֣ר הַ⁠צָּבָ֑א
13.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Please tell her that behold, she has cared all of this care for us, and ask her what we may do for her. Ask her if we may speak for her to the king or to the commander of the army]

Elisha is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [you have taken such good care of us]

16.note: Elisha is using **according to the time of reviving** as a common expression of his culture to mean “when spring comes again.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In the spring of next year]

The Shunammite woman is speaking of herself in the third person as **your maidservant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [to me, your maidservant]

17.note: See how you translated the similar expressions in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [in the spring of the following year]

18.note: The author is using the phrase translated **And it was the day** to introduce a new development within this account of the Shunammite woman. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new development.

19.note: The child is repeating the phrase **My head** in order to intensify his expression of the idea he wishes to convey, which is that his head hurts. If your language can repeat phrases for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Ouch, my head really hurts]

21.note: The author is describing one event before describing another event that preceded it. If it would be helpful in your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened. Alternate translation: [And she went out, and she shut on him]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And she shut the door on him]

22.note: Since the woman has asked for a donkey to ride on, she does not mean that she will literally **run** to see Elisha. Alternate translation: [and let me hurry to the man of God]

23.note: The woman is using **Peace** as a common expression of her culture to mean that she does not want her husband to ask her further questions about why she is going. She wants him to trust her and be confident that she has a good reason. If this expression does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Trust me] or [Do not worry]

24.note: When the author says that **she** (the Shunammite woman) saddled the donkey, he is using her, as one person who was involved in this action, to represent everyone who was involved. It is likely that she directed a servant to saddle the donkey. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And she had a servant saddle the donkey]

If it would appear in your language that the woman was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [Only slacken for me to ride if I tell you to do that]

26.q: וֶ⁠אֱמָר־לָ֗⁠הּ הֲ⁠שָׁל֥וֹם לָ֛⁠ךְ הֲ⁠שָׁל֥וֹם לְ⁠אִישֵׁ֖⁠ךְ הֲ⁠שָׁל֣וֹם לַ⁠יָּ֑לֶד
26.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and ask her whether she and her husband and her child are all right]

Although the word **Peace** is the same one that the ULT translates as **welfare** in the three earlier instances in this verse, the woman seems to be using the word to mean the same thing that she meant in 4:23 when she said it to her husband. She is indicating that she does not want to stop to answer Gehazi’s questions. If this word would not convey that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that would convey that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will explain everything when I get to Elisha]

27.note: Grasping Elisha’s feet was a symbolic action by which the woman showed her desperation and humility as she appealed to him for help. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and she humbly begged him for help by holding onto his feet]

27.q: הַרְפֵּֽה־לָ⁠הּ֙ כִּֽי־נַפְשָׁ֣⁠הּ מָֽרָה־לָ֔⁠הּ וַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ הֶעְלִ֣ים מִמֶּ֔⁠נִּי וְ⁠לֹ֥א הִגִּ֖יד לִֽ⁠י
27.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Her soul is bitter to her, but Yahweh has hidden the reason from me, and he has not declared it to me, so leave her alone]

27.q: וַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ הֶעְלִ֣ים מִמֶּ֔⁠נִּי וְ⁠לֹ֥א הִגִּ֖יד לִֽ⁠י
27.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [but Yahweh has not revealed anything about it to me]

28.note: The Shunammite woman is using the question form for emphasis and to deny that she requested a son. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I did not request a son from my lord!]

Even though the woman is addressing Elisha directly, she is speaking of him in the third person as **my lord** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [from you, my lord]

The woman is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Instead, I said, ‘Do not deceive me’!]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Did I not tell you not to deceive me.] or [Instead, I told you not to deceive me.]

29.q: חֲגֹ֣ר מָתְנֶ֗י⁠ךָ וְ⁠קַ֨ח מִשְׁעַנְתִּ֣⁠י בְ⁠יָדְ⁠ךָ֮ וָ⁠לֵךְ֒
29.note: By telling Gehazi that he should **Gird** his **loins** (that is, tuck his robe into his belt so that he can run), Elisha means that he should hurry. Alternate translation: [Quickly, take my staff in your hand, and go!]

Elisha does not mean that Gehazi would be looking for someone and **find** him somewhere. He means that Gehazi might meet someone on his way to Shunem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [If you meet a man]

In both instances, the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [anyone … anyone]

29.q: לֹ֣א תְבָרְכֶ֔⁠נּוּ וְ⁠כִֽי־יְבָרֶכְ⁠ךָ֥ אִ֖ישׁ לֹ֣א תַעֲנֶ⁠נּ֑וּ
29.note: Elisha assumes that Gehazi will understand that he is not to stop to greet people or exchange greetings, because doing so would delay his urgent mission to the Shunammite woman’s son. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you shall not stop to greet him, and if a man greets you, you shall not stop to exchange greetings with him]

30.note: Following the custom of her culture, the woman is swearing an oath by guaranteeing it by something that she holds sacred and by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). Use a natural way in your language to express an oath. In a context such as this, it may be natural to express just the first part of the condition as a negative statement. Alternate translation: [I swear by Yahweh and by the life of your soul that I will not leave you]

The woman is using one part of Elisha, his **soul**, to mean all of him in the act of being alive. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and your life]

The woman is not saying that she will not leave Mount Carmel. She means that when she goes back to her home, she will not leave Elisha behind. In other words, she is insisting that he come with her. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [if I should leave here without you] or [that I will not leave here without you]

31.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 4:12. Alternate translation: [ahead of them]
The pronoun **he** refers to Gehazi, while the pronoun **him** refers to Elisha. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Gehazi returned to meet Elisha]

The author is speaking as though the young man had been asleep and **did not awaken**. He is using sleep to represent death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [did not come back to life]

32.note: The expression **having been laid** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [on his bed where his mother had laid him]

34.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:4. Alternate translation: [And he got into the bed]

34.q: וַ⁠יָּשֶׂם֩ פִּ֨י⁠ו עַל־פִּ֜י⁠ו וְ⁠עֵינָ֤י⁠ו עַל־עֵינָי⁠ו֙ וְ⁠כַפָּ֣י⁠ו עַל־כפ⁠ו
34.note: Through these actions, Elisha symbolized that he wanted Yahweh to work through him to restore breathing, sight, and feeling to the boy. This was like a prayer that Elisha was acting out. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote.

35.note: This could mean: (1) that Elisha went back down to the house and walked around in it for a while. Alternate translation: [Then Elisha went back down to the house and walked around in it] or (2) that Elisha got off the bed and walked around in the room. Alternate translation: [Then Elisha got off the bed and walked around in the room]

35.q: וַ⁠יֵּ֣לֶךְ בַּ⁠בַּ֗יִת אַחַ֥ת הֵ֨נָּה֙ וְ⁠אַחַ֣ת הֵ֔נָּה
35.note: The author is using **once here and once here** as a common expression of his culture to mean “back and forth.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he walked back and forth in the house]

36.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Gehazi, while the pronoun **him** refers to Elisha. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Gehazi called her, and she came to Elisha]

This is an imperative, but it communicates permission rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates permission. Elisha is assuring the woman that her son is well enough for her to hold him in her arms. Alternate translation: [Your son is well enough for you to pick him up and hold him]

37.note: Be sure that it is clear in your translation that the woman did not fall down accidentally. She knelt down in front of Elisha as a gesture to honor him. She then **prostrated herself** or stretched out flat on the ground to show him even greater honor as a prophet who had done a great miracle by Yahweh’s power. Alternate translation: [and she knelt on the ground in front of Elisha, stretching herself out flat, to honor him greatly]

38.note: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:14. Alternate translation: [in his presence]

39.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and since they did not know, he sliced them into the pot of stew]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [they did not know that the gourds were poisonous]

40.note: The author is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they cried out** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that this action took place at the same time as the men’s action of eating **the stew**. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [as soon as they tasted the stew, that they cried out]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Death**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Something deadly]

42.note: The author is introducing this **man … from Baal Shalishah** as a new participant in the story. This also serves to introduce a new episode in the overall account of how Elisha fed the sons of the prophets during the famine described in 4:38. If your language has its own way of introducing new participants and new episodes, you could use it here in your translation.
The pronoun **he** refers to Elisha. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Elisha said]

43.q: מָ֚ה אֶתֵּ֣ן זֶ֔ה לִ⁠פְנֵ֖י מֵ֣אָה אִ֑ישׁ
43.note: The servant is using the question form to emphasize that the amount of food is not enough. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [This is not enough food to feed a hundred men!]
To translate this expression here and in the next verse, see how you translated the similar expression in 4:12. Alternate translation: [shall I put this in front of] or [shall I serve this to]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that they will have enough to eat, and there will be some left over]

44.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:7. Alternate translation: [according to what Yahweh had said]
